panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a 78-year-old woman showing a classic bull's-eye erythema migrans rash on her lower back/flank. The caption explicitly states 'Classic bull's eye EM' and confirms Lyme disease diagnosis with positive serology (ELISA and western blot). The large, expanding annular erythematous lesion with central clearing is a textbook presentation of early localized Lyme disease. Skin tone is light based on visible adequately lit skin. No ethnicity stated. No image annotations present.
panels.attribution_text: Aucott et al. Diagnostic challenges of early Lyme disease: lessons from a community case series.. BMC infectious diseases 2009. doi:10.1186/1471-2334-9-79. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Classic bull's eye EM with initial misdiagnosis as urinary tract infection. A 78 year old women presented to an urgent care center with 3 days of fever, mild headache and the absence of rhinitis, cough or typical upper respiratory viral symptoms. The physical exam showed a temperature of 102 degrees Fahrenheit and a skin rash was not noted. Urinalysis showed 5–10 WBCs, a diagnosis of pylonephritis was made, and ciprofloxacin was initiated. The patient returned the following day when she noticed a large, red rash on her side. The patient was referred to one of the authors (JA) who confirmed the diagnosis of Lyme disease. Ciprofloxacin was discontinued, doxycycline initiated and the rash resolved. Serology returned with a positive ELISA and confirmatory western blot.
in_text_mentions: While typically circular or oval, it can also be triangular, rectangular or distorted in other ways when occurring in areas such as the neck [6]. Atypical features may include erythema with central induration, urticarial like lesions, confluent red-blue lesions mimicking ecchymosis, vesicles mimicking shingles, and central necrosis mimicking spider bites [6,25,26]. in_text_mentions: se describes a 7-year-old boy from Orange County, South California, USA, who presented with cutaneous LD while in Singapore en route to Manila, Philippines, for a sporting competition. findings.evidence: Caption: 'Clinical appearance of borrelial lymphocytoma at presentation. Solitary erythematous papule with central umbilication located adjacent to the lateral malleolus of the left ankle before treatment.'

panels.rationale: Real patient clinical photograph showing a solitary erythematous papule with central umbilication adjacent to the lateral malleolus of the left ankle, explicitly captioned as borrelial lymphocytoma at presentation before treatment. Borrelial lymphocytoma is a recognized cutaneous manifestation of Lyme borreliosis, and the article title ('Borrelial Lymphocytoma of the Ankle: An Unusual Presentation of Lyme Borreliosis') confirms disease attribution. The ankle location is an unusual site for borrelial lymphocytoma (classically earlobe, nipple, or scrotum), and the title itself flags this as an unusual presentation, so typicality is atypical. Skin appears light (Fitzpatrick I–II) from the visible adequately lit skin. No ethnicity or age stated in caption or in-text mentions. [raw subtype: borrelial_lymphocytoma]

in_text_mentions: While typically circular or oval, it can also be triangular, rectangular or distorted in other ways when occurring in areas such as the neck [6]. Atypical features may include erythema with central induration, urticarial like lesions, confluent red-blue lesions mimicking ecchymosis, vesicles mimicking shingles, and central necrosis mimicking spider bites [6,25,26]. Examples of typical and atypical lesions are shown in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. In our series, the most common misdiagnosis for EM was spider bite, consistent with observations that spider bites may be commonly over-diagnosed [27].

in_text_mentions: A 63-year-old female with unremarkable past medical history presented with persistent fever, headache, and diffuse myalgia for four days after returning from a camping trip in Gainesville, Florida two weeks prior. On presentation, she was febrile at 100.5 F and tachycardic at 127 bpm. She had an erythematous ecchymotic area on her anterior right shin surrounding the location of the reported tick bite (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: A 63-year-old female with unremarkable past medical history presented with persistent fever, headache, and diffuse myalgia for four days after returning from a camping trip in Gainesville, Florida two weeks prior. She also reported noticing a tick on her right leg (Figure 1) and having a pruritic target erythematous lesion after removing it. On presentation, she was febrile at 100.5 F and tachycardic at 127 bpm. She had an erythematous ecchymotic area on her anterior right shin surrounding the location of the reported tick bite (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph from a case report titled 'Atypical Lyme Disease Rash: A Case Report.' It shows a large purplish/erythematous abdominal plaque with central scaling after a tick bite, consistent with atypical erythema migrans in Lyme disease. The disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title and the in-text tick bite/rash description. [raw subtype: erythema_migrans]
panels.attribution_text: Khanna and Goebel. Atypical Lyme Disease Rash: A Case Report.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.54779. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Purplish lesion on the left abdominal wall
in_text_mentions: A 69-year-old West Virginian female, with a history of degenerative joint disease, asthma, breast cancer, and hypothyroidism, sought medical attention because of an itchy rash on her abdomen, which developed six days following a tick bite. On physical exam, her vital signs were normal. Purplish, papular, oval lesions up to 12 centimeters in size were noted on the left lower abdominal wall, spreading from a central area of scaling assumed to be the location of the tick bite (Figure 1).
